name: Boron toxicity
summary: A Cannabis micronutrient toxicity that begins as older- or lower-leaf marginal chlorosis and advances inward to brown or bronze necrosis. Controlled trials link this pattern to elevated boron exposure and leaf-tissue boron, but marginal burn is nonspecific and requires water, input, root-zone, and tissue confirmation.
affectedParts: lower and older fan leaves in the published T1 sequence
upper and lower fan leaves in a separate White Shark trial
interior leaf tissue as injury advances inward
roots, source water, and root zone for causal checks
stages: chronic exposure across multiple growth stages
indicators: Marginal yellowing begins on lower or older fan leaves in the controlled T1 sequence
Yellowing follows the leaflet edge and advances inward toward the midrib
Affected margins turn brown or bronze and become necrotic
Severely chlorotic or necrotic leaves can abscise
A separate three-plant-per-treatment White Shark trial observed margin chlorosis within three weeks, rapidly followed by bronze necrosis on both upper and lower leaves
In a widespread exposure, comparable marginal injury appears across many leaves rather than at one contact point
Elevated boron is documented in representative leaf tissue and a plausible source is identified in nutrient solution, source water, soil, substrate, or amendment
exclusions: Yellowing and necrosis are restricted to the hottest or brightest canopy edge and measured leaf temperature or light exposure explains the pattern
Marginal injury follows a spray, foliar product, fan abrasion, or contact event and stops when the exposure ends
Root-zone EC is high with broad multi-ion tip burn and tissue boron is not elevated
Older leaves show potassium-type saw-tooth marginal yellowing or necrosis and potassium/root-zone evidence explains the pattern better
Margins are damaged but webbing, mites, thrips, fecal spots, chewing, or frass are confirmed
Discrete lesions, halos, fungal structures, or laboratory pathogen results support infectious disease
Cold, waterlogging, drought, unsuitable pH, or root decay is documented and tissue or water analysis does not support excess boron
Purple, bronze, or yellow color is produced only by cultivar pigmentation, senescence, lighting, white balance, or compression artifact

progression.description: Boron accumulates from a source such as nutrient solution, water, substrate, soil, amendment, or calculation error; a photograph alone cannot distinguish it from salinity, potassium disorder, or contact injury.
Lower or older leaflet margins become yellow in the T1 study. In the White Shark DWC trial, marginal chlorosis was visible within three weeks of the 0.05 mM boron treatment.
Marginal chlorosis intensifies and moves inward; tan, brown, or bronze necrosis develops along tips and serrated margins.
Leaf margins become broadly necrotic, remaining tissue can be severely chlorotic, and some affected leaves may abscise.
Use new-lesion rate, new leaf quality, water and root-zone testing, and follow-up tissue boron to assess response; existing necrotic margins will not recover.

lookAlikes: Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm boron toxicity from marginal burn, bronze color, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected-toxicity label until elevated boron and a plausible exposure source are linked to the photographed plant.

Capture serial whole-plant, upper- and lower-canopy, leaf upper-surface, leaf underside, margin close-up, root, and root-zone views under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched healthy same-cultivar plant.

Record leaf node and physiological age, cultivar, stage, fertilizer and amendment formulations, mixing calculations, source-water history, irrigation and drainage, root-zone pH, EC, water content, and temperature.

Submit representative leaf tissue from a defined node and maturity class to an agricultural laboratory; interpret boron with a Cannabis-, stage-, plant-part-, and method-appropriate reference rather than treating 671.75 mg per kg from the T1 experiment as a universal threshold.

Test source water, stock solutions, final nutrient solution, soil or substrate, and relevant amendments for boron and salinity; inspect dosing equipment and reverse-osmosis performance where applicable.

Inspect both leaf surfaces and roots and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when pests, foliar injury, or pathogens remain plausible; improvement after source correction supports but does not alone prove the original causal label.
immediateActions: Stop discretionary boron-containing additives while preserving product labels, batch records, solution samples, pre-treatment images, and representative tissue for testing.
Verify source-water, stock, final-solution, root-zone, and tissue results before flushing or changing the complete nutrient program.
Separate suspect plants from training-ground-truth collections until the exposure and laboratory evidence are linked.
correctivePlan: Remove or correct the verified boron source and restore a balanced crop- and stage-appropriate nutrient solution using current local agronomic guidance.
Correct documented salinity, drainage, irrigation, pH, temperature, or root-health problems without assuming that every burned margin was caused by boron.
Track new growth, new-lesion rate, water or solution boron, EC and pH, and follow-up tissue results; reopen differentials if the expected exposure-response relationship is absent.
prevention: Test source water periodically for boron and salinity, especially after treatment-system, well, or reverse-osmosis changes.
Use verified mixing calculations and calibrated dosing equipment for micronutrient concentrates; record lot, concentration, date, and plant group.
Keep same-cultivar healthy references and consistent leaf-node tissue-sampling procedures so changes in leaf age or genotype are not mistaken for toxicity.
warnings: The T1 study induced toxicity with tenfold boron in one silica-sand system; its seven-week timing and 671.75 mg per kg tissue value are experiment-specific, not universal thresholds.
The White Shark report used three clones per treatment in deep-water culture; its three-week onset and canopy-wide distribution require replication across cultivars and production systems.
Marginal chlorosis and necrosis are highly nonspecific and must not become image-only ground truth.
The two source trials did not justify a universal yield-loss estimate; severe-looking leaf injury did not correspond to a clear yield loss in the small White Shark trial.
The CC BY figure contains both manganese- and boron-toxicity columns and is excluded from automated training until panel-level crops, labels, and dataset splits are reviewed.
The Niagara College project captured weekly 360-degree videos, but no original asset URLs or reuse license are publicly exposed; none are admitted as video references.
All symptom-only samples remain low confidence and require human review.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Cannabis sativa T1 plants were grown in silica sand with a complete modified Hoagland solution or a solution withholding one nutrient, observed daily, photographed through initial, intermediate, and advanced symptoms, and sampled at first symptom expression for most-recent-mature-leaf tissue analysis.

Nitrogen-withheld plants developed symptoms after six weeks: slight stunting and lower-foliage paling progressed upward into middle foliage, then affected leaves became fully yellow, necrotic, and abscised.

At first symptom expression, nitrogen-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.62% nitrogen dry weight compared with 4.28% in controls, and treated plants produced 50% less dry biomass under the experiment conditions.
Only the left column of Figure 2 represents nitrogen deficiency; the center and right columns are phosphorus and calcium deficiency and must retain separate labels.
The one-cultivar, silica-sand, complete-withholding experiment does not establish universal onset timing, tissue thresholds, production symptoms, or response to partial nitrogen limitation.

Phosphorus-withheld plants first showed slight stunting and irregular olive-green spots on lower and older leaflets after seven weeks; spots enlarged, appeared sunken and almost wet, developed some marginal necrosis, and advanced to extensive olive spotting and large necrotic portions.

At first phosphorus-deficiency symptom expression, phosphorus-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.09% phosphorus dry weight compared with 0.43% in controls, a 79% difference under the experiment conditions.

The study used one cultivar, began nutrient withholding at transplant, and reported no statistically significant biomass difference for phosphorus-withheld plants at the symptom-onset harvest, so its timing, tissue value, and appearance are not universal diagnostic thresholds.
Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced nitrogen-, phosphorus-, and calcium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1.

In calcium-withheld T1 plants, symptoms appeared after five weeks as slight stunting and irregular growing tips and newly expanding leaves; leaflet bases stayed narrow and paler than tips, then basal and interveinal chlorosis, marginal necrosis, distorted geometry, growing-tip death, and axillary branching developed.

At first calcium-deficiency symptom expression, most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.39% calcium dry weight compared with 3.73% in controls, but the one-cultivar silica-sand withholding experiment does not establish a universal tissue threshold or field sequence.

Iron-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks: slight marginal yellowing, especially near leaflet bases, progressed to interveinal chlorosis on growing-tip and newly expanding leaves and spread through the upper half while middle and lower foliage remained healthy dark green.

At first iron-deficiency symptom expression, iron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 60.08 mg/kg iron compared with 111.75 mg/kg in controls, 46% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.
Figure 6 is a CC BY 4.0 composite with initial, intermediate, and advanced iron-deficiency images in its left column and zinc-deficiency images in its right column.

Manganese-withheld T1 plants developed bright-yellow netted interveinal chlorosis on upper and central foliage after six weeks; the netting began near leaflet midribs, spread toward margins, retained green veins, and later developed small tan necrotic regions.

At first manganese-deficiency symptom expression, manganese-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 7.56 mg/kg manganese compared with 29.40 mg/kg in controls, 74% lower under the experiment conditions; dry biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

The control manganese concentration was itself below the cited general crop survey range, and the study used one cultivar in silica sand with complete withholding, so neither treatment value is a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced manganese-, boron-, and copper-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its left column represents manganese deficiency.

Copper-withheld T1 plants first developed visible symptoms after nine weeks, beginning with slight whole-plant stunting and mild distortion of newer and expanding leaves, especially narrowed and slightly yellow leaflet bases.

As copper-withholding symptoms advanced, basal narrowing and distortion intensified, marginal interveinal chlorosis developed, and the whole leaf progressed to fine interveinal chlorosis with slightly inward- and downward-curled margins and reduced turgidity.

At first copper-deficiency symptom expression, copper-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 1.41 mg/kg copper compared with 4.65 mg/kg in controls, 70% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 45% less biomass.

The control copper concentration of 4.65 mg/kg was itself slightly below the general crop survey range cited by the authors, and the one-cultivar complete-withholding result does not establish a universal Cannabis threshold.

The published Figure 4 caption and column labels identify initial, intermediate, and advanced copper-deficiency panels in the right column, although the copper subsection text cites Figure 5; Figure 5 is captioned as manganese- and boron-toxicity progression, so this source-level numbering inconsistency must remain attached to copper panel review.

Magnesium-withheld T1 plants first developed slight interveinal yellowing on lower and older foliage after seven weeks; the contrast between green veins and yellow interveinal tissue intensified and some regions became necrotic.

At first magnesium-deficiency symptom expression, magnesium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.12% magnesium compared with 0.61% in controls, 80% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly at that harvest.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite showing initial, intermediate, and advanced sulfur-, magnesium-, and potassium-deficiency phenotypes in Cannabis sativa T1; only its center column represents magnesium deficiency.

Potassium-withheld T1 plants first developed yellowing at leaflet margins and saw-tooth serrations on lower and older foliage after nine weeks; yellowing intensified and moved inward toward the midrib, followed by tan necrosis concentrated along serrated margins.

At first potassium-deficiency symptom expression, potassium-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.41% potassium compared with 2.85% in controls, 86% lower under the experiment conditions; treated plants produced 27% less biomass.

Figure 3 is a CC BY 4.0 composite whose right column shows initial, intermediate, and advanced potassium-deficiency phenotypes; the sulfur and magnesium columns are separate diagnoses and the asset is indexed once under the magnesium record to avoid duplicate media hashes.

Zinc-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after nine weeks as marginal yellowing on newer and expanding leaves, concentrated along leaflet margins and toothed portions; tan, irregularly shaped marginal necrosis developed as the disorder progressed.

At first zinc-deficiency symptom expression, zinc-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 10.70 mg/kg zinc compared with 25.33 mg/kg in controls, 58% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

Sulfur-withheld T1 plants first developed symptoms after seven weeks as slight overall yellowing, especially in the middle canopy and at leaflet bases; yellowing intensified at leaflet bases and on newly expanding leaves, then advanced to very pale yellow tissue around the midrib and leaflet bases.

At first sulfur-deficiency symptom expression, sulfur-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 0.11% sulfur compared with 0.41% in controls, 73% lower under the experiment conditions; biomass did not differ significantly from the control at that harvest.

sources.title: Documentation of Boron Deficiency and Phytotoxicity in Cannabis sativa to Aid in Development of the GrowDoc Application
sources.organization: Horticultural & Environmental Sciences Innovation Centre, Niagara College
sources.publisher: Niagara College Horticultural & Environmental Sciences Innovation Centre
supportedClaims: Three White Shark Cannabis clones per treatment were grown in deep-water culture with 0.0063 mM boron control solution, zero-boron solution, or 0.05 mM boron toxicity solution; pH and EC were monitored and mature leaf tissue was analyzed by an external laboratory.

The 0.05 mM treatment developed marginal chlorosis within three weeks, quickly followed by bronze necrosis; the injury occurred on both upper and lower leaves and affected nearly every leaf in the three treated plants.
The boron-toxicity tissue analysis was elevated while other measured nutrients were described as sufficient, strengthening the treatment-to-symptom link under this small controlled trial.

In this trial, toxicity caused persistent leaf-margin injury but height, SPAD, yield, and measured THC remained close to controls, showing that visual severity must not be converted into a universal yield-loss estimate.

Researchers captured weekly close-ups, whole-plant photographs, and 360-degree video, but the public report does not expose original video asset URLs or a reuse license; those unlinked assets cannot be admitted to this dataset.

media.alt: Six-panel Cannabis nutrient-toxicity figure with manganese toxicity in the left column, boron toxicity in the right column, and initial, intermediate, and advanced rows
media.caption: Controlled-study composite. The right column shows boron-toxicity progression from marginal yellowing to inward-spreading chlorosis and advanced brown necrosis; the left manganese column is a separate diagnosis.
media.creator: Paul Cockson, Hunter Landis, Turner Smith, Kristin Hicks, and Brian E. Whipker

useLimitations: Scientific reference only until the right-side boron panels are separately cropped, bounded, and assigned a dataset split.
The composite contains two diagnosis classes: manganese toxicity in the left column and boron toxicity in the right; do not train or infer one label from the full image.
One cultivar and tenfold-supply protocol do not establish universal symptom timing, tissue thresholds, or production-system response.
